name: Awadh State
info: A Mughal province in North India that its nawabs turned into an independent kingdom, then a British protectorate, until the East India Company annexed it in 1856.

facts.capital: Ayodhya, then Faizabad (from 1740); the Company's Residents sat at Lucknow
facts.founder: Saadat Ali Khan I, appointed Subahdar of Oudh in 1722
facts.predecessor: Oudh Subah of the Mughal Empire
facts.successor: North Western Provinces and Oudh (British India)

t: Saadat Ali Khan I, appointed Subahdar of Oudh in 1722, subdued local powers and consolidated Oudh as a state as Mughal authority declined.
The East India Company's victory at the Battle of Buxar in 1764 began a long period of British interference, subsidies and cessions of land.
Lord Dalhousie deposed Wajid Ali Shah and annexed Oudh on 7 February 1856, on the grounds of alleged misrule; Oudh rose against British rule in the rebellion of 1857.
dyk: Ghazi-ud-Din Haidar Shah instituted the Oudh Bequest, fixed payments by the British to the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala, paid as interest on a loan Oudh made to the Company in 1825.
ev: Saadat Ali Khan I is appointed Subahdar of Oudh Subah and subdues the Shaikhzadas of Lucknow and Raja Mohan Singh of Tiloi

sections.foundation:
The name Oudh, now obsolete, was once the anglicized name of the state, also written historically as Oudhe. Oudh Subah was one of the original twelve subahs that Akbar established in his administrative reforms of 1572–1580, divided into sarkars and these into parganas. At its creation it consisted of five sarkars subdivided into 38 parganas. On 9 September 1722 Saadat Ali Khan I was appointed Subahdar of Oudh Subah, succeeding Girdhar Bahadur. He at once subdued the autonomous Shaikhzadas of Lucknow and Raja Mohan Singh of Tiloi, consolidating Oudh as a state.

In 1728 Oudh acquired Varanasi, Jaunpur and the surrounding lands from the Mughal noble Rustam Ali Khan, and established stable revenue collection there after quelling the chief of Azamgarh, Mahabat Khan. As the Mughal Empire dissolved and governors in Bengal and the Deccan asserted their autonomy, and as the Maratha Empire rose, the rulers of Oudh gradually affirmed their own sovereignty. In 1740 Saadat Khan's successor Safdar Jang moved the capital from Ayodhya to Faizabad.
sections.socioeconomy:
Oudh governed the fertile lands of the Central and Lower Doab and lay in a prosperous region; the affluence in which its nawabs lived drew the attention of the British East India Company, and the Nawab of Oudh was counted among the richest princes. In the early eighteenth century its population was estimated at 3 million. Over the course of the century Lucknow and Varanasi grew into metropolises of over 200,000 people at the expense of Agra and Delhi. The land on the banks of the Yamuna suffered frequent dry spells, while the Baiswara did not.

Although Oudh was ruled by Muslims, roughly four fifths of its population were Hindus. Allahabad, Varanasi and Ayodhya were important pilgrimage sites for followers of Hinduism and other Dharmic religions, and the town of Bahraich was revered by some Muslims. The Nawab paid for and erected a Residency in Lucknow as part of a wider programme of civic improvements. Feudatory estates, the taluqdaris or parganas, included Amethi, Balrampur, Mahmudabad, Pratapgarh, Nanpara and Tulsipur.
sections.military:
Saadat Khan mobilised Oudh in 1739 to defend against Nader Shah's invasion of India and was captured at the Battle of Karnal; he tried to negotiate with Nader Shah but died in Delhi. Safdar Jang continued an expansionist policy, promising military protection to Bengal in exchange for the forts of Rohtasgarh and Chunar, and annexing portions of Farrukhabad, ruled by Muhammad Khan Bangash, with Mughal military aid.

The turning point came at the Battle of Buxar in 1764, when the East India Company defeated the alliance of Shuja-ud-Daula and the deposed nawab of Bengal, Mir Kasim. The British occupied the fort at Chunar, and Shuja-ud-Daula paid an indemnity of 5 million rupees. With Company troops, paid for by Oudh, and Company aid in the First Rohilla War, Oudh gained the whole of Rohilkhand and the Middle Doab in 1774, leaving only Rampur State as a Rohilla enclave. Thereafter Oudh relied on British troops in its service, whose cost the Company repeatedly raised.
sections.governance:
The rulers of Oudh came from a Shia Muslim Sayyid family of Nishapur in Persia, descended from Musa al-Kadhim, and also traced descent on the paternal line to the Kara Koyunlu through Qara Yusuf; they were renowned for their secularism and broad outlook, and promoted Shia as the state religion. All used the title Nawab until Ghazi-ud-Din Haidar Shah took that of Badshah in 1819. Safdar Jang controlled the ruler of Delhi, placing Ahmad Shah Bahadur on the Mughal throne, and Shuja-ud-Daula became vazir to Shah Alam II in 1762.

From 1773 Warren Hastings appointed a resident, Nathaniel Middleton, at Lucknow to shape Oudh's policy and direct its internal affairs. Asaf-ud-Daula acceded with British aid, and from then on Oudh consistently complied with the Company's demands; his reliance on British aid made his rule essentially a puppet regime. Saadat Ali Khan II owed his throne in 1798 to Sir John Shore's proclamation in Lucknow. A Maratha embassy under the Vakil of the Peshwa also sat at the court until the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
sections.impact:
For the East India Company, Oudh served above all as a buffer state protecting the frontiers of Bengal and their trade there, and against Maratha interests. The Treaty of Benares of 1765 gave British traders special privileges and exemptions from many customs duties, which led to tension as British monopolies were established. In the Treaty of Benares of 1773 Shuja-ud-Daula bought the provinces of Kora and Allahabad from the British for 50 lakh rupees, a policy of Warren Hastings that was unpopular among the rest of the Company's leadership.

The subsidies grew steadily. The Treaty of Benares of 1775 ceded the sarkars of Benares, Ghazipur, Chunar and Jaunpur; the Treaty of Chunar of 1781 failed to reduce the British troops in Oudh's service; and a treaty of 21 February 1798 raised the subsidy to 70 lakh rupees a year. Oudh's wealth also reached beyond India: the Oudh Bequest, set up by Ghazi-ud-Din Haidar Shah, made fixed payments to the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala as interest on the Third Oudh Loan of 1825.
sections.decline:
In 1801, under pressure from Lord Wellesley, Saadat Ali Khan II ceded the whole of Rohilkhand, the Lower Doab and the sarkar of Gorakhpur in lieu of the annual tribute. The cession halved the state, left it surrounded by British territory and useless as a buffer, and bound it to a government serving its people; the British later cited failure to meet this demand to justify annexation. Oudh became a British protectorate in May 1816, and further areas were ceded through the early 1800s.

On 7 February 1856 Lord Dalhousie deposed Wajid Ali Shah and annexed Oudh under the Doctrine of Lapse on the grounds of alleged internal misrule. In the Indian Rebellion of 1857, from 5 July 1857 to 3 March 1858, Begum Hazrat Mahal proclaimed her son Birjis Qadr Wali of Awadh and ruled as regent; the British reestablished their rule over the next eighteen months, and rebels fought on until 1859. Oudh was merged into the North-Western Provinces and Oudh, later the United Provinces, which became Uttar Pradesh in 1950.

summary: Oudh grew from a Mughal subah, consolidated by Saadat Ali Khan I from 1722, into a wealthy independent kingdom of the Doab with its capital at Faizabad. After the Battle of Buxar in 1764 the East India Company drew ever more land and money from it, made it a protectorate in 1816 and annexed it in 1856.

notes: The article is thin (about 11 KB) and lists no references, so references are empty. It says the 1858 upheaval and the 'Bombay Army' campaign, which may be confused; I followed the dates of the Rebellion section (1857-1858, guerrilla fighting to 1859). Capital: the lead says Faizabad, the history says Safdar Jang moved it from Ayodhya to Faizabad in 1740; Lucknow is given only as the Residents' seat. 'Doctrine of Lapse' is the article's wording, though it also says the grounds were misrule.
